decisions.why: Translating only the short questions gets most of the benefit for a tiny cost, and full translations stay possible later.
decisions.learn: Cross-lingual retrieval, doc2query, multilingual embeddings.

decisions.title: Entry metadata policy
decisions.question: Which front-matter fields of an entry may be indexed and shown?
decisions.context: Some fields describe the work (title, type, domain, period, role, stack, patterns) and help retrieval. Others are provenance for the owner (sources, conflicts, public names, confidence) and may hint at internal details. A confidence of medium means only documents, not code, support a detail.

options.label: Index descriptive fields, keep provenance private
options.description: Index title, type, domain, period, role, stack, patterns; keep sources, conflicts, public_names and confidence private; hedge on medium confidence.

options.label: Index everything
options.description: All front matter goes into chunks.
cons: Conflict notes and sources may leak internal details

options.label: Index body text only
options.description: No front matter.

decisions.why: Descriptive fields improve answers, while provenance is for the owner's review, not for visitors.
decisions.learn: Data classification, contextual headers.

decisions.title: Answer feedback loop
decisions.question: How should visitor thumbs up and down be collected and used?
decisions.context: Feedback attached to the trace of the answer it rates shows exactly what went wrong. An annotation queue is a review list in LangSmith where the owner triages runs. Promoting confirmed failures into the eval battery means the same failure cannot silently come back: the human-feedback-to-evals loop.

options.label: LangSmith feedback + annotation queue + promotion into the battery
options.description: Signed run tokens, one rating per run per session, thumbs-down and a 10% sample of thumbs-up queued for weekly review.
cons: Optional comments are personal data in a third-party tool

options.label: Own feedback table and admin page
options.description: Store and review locally.
cons: No trace next to the rating

options.label: No feedback
options.description: Skip it.
cons: Evals only reflect the owner's guesses

decisions.why: It turns real visitors' judgments into regression tests with very little code, and it never changes behavior automatically, so it cannot be gamed.
decisions.learn: Human in the loop, annotation queues, data flywheel.

decisions.title: Semantic cache
decisions.question: Should repeated questions be answered from a cache, and how is that kept safe and fresh?
decisions.context: A semantic cache serves a stored answer when a new question means the same as one already answered, saving cost and latency. It differs from prompt caching, which only makes the prompt cheaper while the model still generates. The risks are serving stale answers after content changes and cache poisoning, where an attacker gets a bad answer stored for everyone.

options.label: pgvector cache with source-id invalidation and a popularity threshold
options.description: First-turn CV answers only; key includes locale, index and prompt version; content events delete answers citing changed sources; served only after two sessions asked; 7-day TTL.

options.label: Exact-match cache
options.description: Normalized question text only.

options.label: A cache service with off-the-shelf libraries
options.description: Redis semantic cache.

options.label: No semantic cache
options.description: Prompt caching only.

decisions.why: Precise invalidation and the popularity threshold handle the two real risks, and pgvector is already there; the eval battery measures hit and false-hit rates before it goes live.
decisions.learn: Cache-aside, invalidation, TTL, cache poisoning.

decisions.title: Multi-agent supervisor
decisions.question: How should requests be routed between the CV agent and the recruiter agent?
decisions.context: A supervisor is a node that decides which specialist agent handles a turn and hands control to it, then gets it back. Specialists can each have their own prompt, tools, limits and evaluations. Anthropic's guidance is to add agents only when the jobs genuinely differ; here they do.

options.label: Hand-built supervisor reusing the guard classification
options.description: Routing from the guard's structured output (no extra model call), handoffs to two subgraphs, confirmation before analyzing a pasted JD.

options.label: One graph with branches
options.description: The earlier design.
cons: One prompt grows to serve two jobs

options.label: Swarm of agents handing off to each other
options.description: Peer-to-peer handoffs.
cons: Harder to bound and reason about

options.label: A prebuilt supervisor helper
options.description: Library-provided supervisor.
cons: Hides the routing the owner wants to learn

decisions.why: Building the supervisor by hand on top of an existing classification teaches the pattern at zero extra runtime cost.
decisions.learn: Supervisor, handoff, router, subgraph.

decisions.title: Chaos testing
decisions.question: How should the claim "the site stays up and loses no messages when a service or the broker stops" be proven?
decisions.context: Chaos engineering deliberately breaks parts of a system to check that it behaves as designed. It starts from a steady-state hypothesis: a measurable definition of "fine", such as every page answering 200 and every contact message delivered exactly once after recovery. A scripted test makes the check repeatable instead of a one-off exercise.

options.label: Scripted chaos test in staging
options.description: Synthetic traffic, stop agent then RabbitMQ for two minutes each, restart, check the steady-state hypothesis, publish the report.
cons: A script and fixtures to maintain

options.label: Manual game day only
options.description: Do it by hand once (WP-27).

options.label: Continuous chaos in production
options.description: Random failures in production.

options.label: Network faults with Toxiproxy
options.description: Latency and dropped connections.
cons: More setup; better as a later extension

decisions.why: A scripted test turns resilience from a claim into a check that runs before every risky release, and its results become content for the site.
decisions.learn: Chaos engineering, steady-state hypothesis, blast radius, game day.

decisions.title: Work tracking from roadmap to tickets
decisions.question: Where should the roadmap live as an epic and tickets?
decisions.context: An epic groups the whole roadmap; each work package becomes a ticket with acceptance criteria (definition of ready) and a checklist for done. Linking tickets to pull requests and releases gives traceability: from a changelog line back to the decision and the ticket. Once the repo is public, the ticket history also shows reviewers how the work was run.

options.label: GitHub Issues with sub-issues, a Project board and milestones
options.description: One epic with a sub-issue per WP, templates, labels, phase milestones, a Project with WP id, tag, size and phase fields; PRs close issues; release-please links them.

options.label: Linear
options.description: A dedicated issue tracker with GitHub integration.

options.label: Local backlog
options.description: Markdown or the firstmate task tool.
cons: No board, no automatic PR linking

decisions.why: Decided by the owner on 2026-10-02: GitHub Issues with sub-issues, a Project board and milestones, which also shows the owner working with those tools. Linear was discarded because it adds a tool and keeps the history outside the repo, where reviewers of the public repo will not see it; a local backlog was discarded because it has no board, no automatic PR linking and no recognizable lifecycle to show.
decisions.learn: Epics and sub-issues, definition of ready and done, traceability.

decisions.title: Site positioning
decisions.question: What should the site say the owner is, in one sentence?
decisions.context: Positioning is the one sentence a visitor remembers after ten seconds. The site serves several audiences: the internal agentic team, hiring managers at product companies looking for backend, platform or full-stack engineers, recruiters who skim, and peers who read the code. A positioning tied to one team narrows every other door, while the evidence can still show depth in each area.

options.label: Broad engineer with applied AI as one strong pillar
options.description: A backend-focused full-stack engineer who designs, tests, ships and operates whole systems, with applied AI as one of them.
pros: The AI work still stands out as a pillar

options.label: Agentic AI engineer
options.description: The site leads with AI agents as the identity.
cons: Undersells the backend, infra and testing work

options.label: Full-stack generalist
options.description: No specialty named.
cons: Hides the backend depth and the AI work

decisions.why: It matches the owner's stated intent: the move to the agentic team stays well supported by the AI pillar, while the same page works for any backend, platform or full-stack role.
decisions.learn: Positioning, audience analysis.

decisions.title: Home page and hero structure
decisions.question: What should the home page show first?
decisions.context: Most visitors never type into a chat box, so the first screen must show the breadth on its own. A proof-pillar strip is a row of short cards, one per skill area, each linking to the evidence that proves it. The agent stays visible as one inviting entry point, and the page must read as complete when the agent is resting.

options.label: Positioning + proof pillars + case studies, agent as one entry point
options.description: Headline and one line of proof, the pillar strip, featured case studies, the experience timeline with Ask about this, an Ask me prompt among them.
cons: The agent is no longer the first thing you see

options.label: Agent-first hero
options.description: The chat prompt is the hero.
cons: Only visitors who type see the breadth
Couples the story to the agent

options.label: Classic CV-first home
options.description: Agent only on its own page.

decisions.why: It lets a skimming reviewer see every pillar immediately and keeps the agent as a strong, optional way to go deeper.
decisions.learn: Information hierarchy, progressive disclosure, graceful degradation.

decisions.title: Launch scope balance
decisions.question: With the agent as one pillar among several, what should be in the launch scope?
decisions.context: The launch scope is about 102 focused days, and much of the added work deepens the AI pillar. The recruiter agent and the supervisor deepen applied AI only, while the Under the hood page proves architecture, reliability, CI/CD and infrastructure at once. Work moved to right after launch still ships; it just stops delaying the launch.

options.label: Launch scope as planned
options.description: Everything currently marked launch scope, about 102 days.

options.label: Move the recruiter agent and supervisor after launch, keep Under the hood
options.description: WP-37 and WP-47 move to right after launch; about 97 days.
cons: Recruiter mode arrives a little later

options.label: Full cut line
options.description: Also move the Under the hood page after launch; about 94.5 days.
cons: Loses the page that proves several pillars at once

decisions.why: It removes the work that deepens only one pillar from the critical path and keeps the page that proves many pillars, in line with the broad positioning.
decisions.learn: Scope management, critical path.

decisions.title: Case-study lineup
decisions.question: Which case studies appear, and in what order?
decisions.context: Case studies are the deepest evidence on the site, so they should together cover every proof pillar. Order signals priority: the first one is the story most visitors read. Leading with AI would repeat the coupling the owner wants to avoid.

options.label: Four case studies covering every pillar
options.description: jadero.dev itself (architecture, messaging, testing, CI/CD, infrastructure, applied AI), El Refugio (product delivery and frontend craft, years in production), the Claude Code framework (developer tooling and engineering process, public-level), LangChainAssistant (applied AI on a NestJS backend).
pros: Every pillar has a case study
AI appears in two but leads none

options.label: AI-led order
options.description: LangChainAssistant and the framework first.
pros: Strongest signal for the agentic team
cons: Couples the site to one move

options.label: Three case studies
options.description: LangChainAssistant moves to selected projects.
cons: Less AI depth on the site

decisions.why: It puts the broadest, most current proof first and still gives the AI work two strong appearances.
decisions.learn: Evidence mapping, narrative order.

manualActions.what: Decide D-1 to D-53 in the plan review, and check which GitHub plan the account is on (it affects D-29).
manualActions.why: Nothing is built before the architecture decisions are made, and repo visibility depends on the plan.

manualActions.what: Create Anthropic Console workspaces (production, CI evals, development), one API key per workspace, and set a monthly spend limit on each (production about USD 20).
manualActions.why: Separate keys and limits bound the cost of a leak or an attack per environment.

manualActions.what: Create a Voyage AI account and API keys (production, CI).
manualActions.why: Embeddings and reranking provider; the free 200M tokens cover this corpus.

manualActions.what: Optionally create an OpenAI project with a key and a budget to prove the alternative adapters.
manualActions.when: WP-19, only if testing the alternative
manualActions.why: The provider-agnostic design is only proven once a second provider passes the contract suite.

manualActions.what: Create a LangSmith account in the EU region, one project per environment, and API keys.
manualActions.why: Agent tracing and evals.

manualActions.what: Create a Cloudflare account and a Turnstile widget for jadero.dev, new.jadero.dev and localhost; store the site key and secret.
manualActions.why: Bot protection for the contact form and the chat.

manualActions.what: Create a Resend account, verify the sending domain with the DNS records it asks for (SPF, DKIM), create an API key, and choose the address that receives notifications.
manualActions.why: Contact notifications; Hetzner blocks outbound ports 25 and 465.

manualActions.what: Create GitHub OAuth apps for the admin login (development, staging, production callback URLs) and note your numeric GitHub user id for the allow-list.
manualActions.why: Admin authentication allows exactly one immutable user id.

manualActions.what: Create a Tailscale account, install it on the server and your machine, and create an auth key or OAuth client for GitHub Actions.
manualActions.why: Deploys and SSH without a public port 22.

manualActions.what: In the Hetzner Cloud Console, create the Cloud Firewall (80 and 443 only) and attach it to the server; optionally enable server backups and order a Storage Box for offsite backups.
manualActions.why: Docker can bypass ufw; the Cloud Firewall filters before traffic reaches the server.

manualActions.what: Add DNS records: new., admin., stats., status. (later staging., mcp., lab.) pointing to the server, plus Resend's records.
manualActions.why: Every subdomain needs a record before certbot can issue its certificate.

manualActions.what: On the server, run the setup steps the agent prepares (users, Docker, compose projects, nginx vhosts, certbot), because agents never touch the server.
manualActions.why: Server administration stays with the owner.

manualActions.what: Configure the GitHub repo: protect main, squash merges with the PR title as the commit, Actions permission to write packages, CI secrets (Tailscale key, CI provider keys, LangSmith key), and after going public, environments with required reviewers.
manualActions.why: CI, releases and deploys depend on these settings.

manualActions.what: Create a read-only GHCR token for the server to pull images.
manualActions.why: The server must pull private images without broader GitHub access.

manualActions.what: Create a free OpenTelemetry backend account (for example Grafana Cloud) and an OTLP token.
manualActions.why: Cross-service traces and metrics without heavy software on the server.

manualActions.what: Create a free external uptime check on the home page and the API health.
manualActions.why: Uptime Kuma cannot report its own server going down.

manualActions.what: Pick the visual direction from the three mockups.
manualActions.why: Frontend is result-only; the owner chooses.

manualActions.what: Provide a professional photo and project screenshots or short GIFs (old demos are dead).
manualActions.why: Project cards and the hero need real media.

manualActions.what: Write the CV (Layer A) and the knowledge entries (Layer B) in at least en and es, link each CV bullet to its entries, and fill the private denylist of internal terms.
manualActions.why: The agent can only answer from approved content; the denylist protects employer details.

manualActions.what: Approve each knowledge entry per locale with the checklist, confirming it is public-level, and approve the public-level text about the current role and the framework case study.
manualActions.why: Only owner-approved entries are ever indexed or published.

manualActions.what: Review the privacy notice (Umami, LangSmith, AI providers, contact form retention).
manualActions.why: Visitor messages are personal data.

manualActions.what: Make the repository public after the gitleaks history scan comes back clean.
manualActions.why: Unlocks environments and code scanning on GitHub Free; the code is the evidence.

manualActions.what: Approve the cutover, then stop the old pm2 services and revoke the old reCAPTCHA keys in the Google admin console.
manualActions.why: The old site and its backend retire with v2.

manualActions.what: Optionally clean up the old GitHub repos the site links to (READMEs, dead demo links, homepage fields, the Docker repo's committed .env files) and refresh the profile README.
manualActions.why: The site sends reviewers to these repos.

manualActions.what: Work through each learning gate: read the explainer, ask until it is clear, decide, and explain the design back at the end of each learning work package.
manualActions.why: Learning is a hard requirement; the gate only works with the owner's decision.

manualActions.what: Decide D-54 to D-72 together with the rest in the plan review, including whether to apply the suggested cut line (recruiter agent, supervisor and Under the hood right after launch).
manualActions.why: The additions add about 20 days before launch.

manualActions.what: Deliver the knowledge entries in the agreed file format, keep public_names accurate, and set approved: true only on entries you have checked.
manualActions.why: Only approved entries are ever imported as approved and indexed.

manualActions.what: Review and approve the roughly 30 eval battery items, and write the adversarial and out-of-scope items by hand.
manualActions.why: The battery gates every prompt and model change.

manualActions.what: Review the annotation queue weekly and promote confirmed failures into the battery.
manualActions.why: This is what turns visitor feedback into regression tests.

manualActions.what: Write the first /now text and edit a journal post at the end of each learning work package.
manualActions.why: The journal is published in the owner's voice.

manualActions.what: Create an Uptime Kuma status page for the Under the hood data (service names only).
manualActions.why: The page reads public status data, not internal monitors.

manualActions.what: Try the public MCP from your own MCP client and, if wanted, list it in a public MCP directory.
manualActions.why: Proves the AI-client experience end to end.

manualActions.what: Consent to the admin MCP client on first use and decide whether the admin MCP is reachable only over Tailscale.
manualActions.why: OAuth consent is a human act; network exposure is the owner's call.

manualActions.what: Curate the framework catalog: names and generic descriptions only, no company material, then approve each item.
manualActions.why: Nothing from the framework repository may be read by jadero.dev code.

manualActions.what: Create the GitHub Project, milestones and labels (or approve the agent doing it with gh), and keep issue text public-level.
manualActions.why: Issues become public with the repo.

manualActions.what: Confirm the job-description retention choice and that the privacy notice covers recruiter mode, feedback comments and the semantic cache.
manualActions.why: These features process visitor-provided text.
